newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian call ends easy, gilts steady in poor trade.
newsitem.headline: Indian call ends easy, gilts steady in poor trade.

text.p: Indian call money ended Monday at 4.75-5.0 percent, marginally down from the weekend close of 5.0-5.25 percent in conditions of good liquidity, dealers said.
They said supply of funds was good on inflows over the past few days and further inflows were expected in the next few days.

"About 17 billion rupees came in during the last three days through interest payments on government securities and redemption of securities which had matures," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "A further 8.5 billion is expected this week."
He said there was little likelihood of call money rising sharply despite a bond auction slated for May 28.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) auctions 30 billion rupees of three-year central government bonds on Wednesday.
"Immediately after the auction, call money may rise on sentiment," the dealer said. "But with liquidity as good as it is, rates should not rise much above 6.0 percent."
Dealers said heavy spot-dollar purchases by RBI on Monday will also add to domestic liquidity.

They estimated RBI purchases on Monday to be between $150 million and $300 million as it intervened to stem the rupee's rise against the US currency. The Indian rupee ended Monday at 35.78/79 per dollar against the weekend close of 35.75/755.
"This (purchase) will inject rupees into the system on Wednesday and should balance the outflows to some extent," said a dealer at a foreign bank.
Prices of government securities were largely steady in dull trade, dealers said.
They said there was selling pressure as traders sought to raise funds to participate in the bond auction but trade was poor as there were few buyers.
"Most market players are keeping funds aside for the auction," said a dealer. "Fresh positions will be taken only after the auction."

Dealers said the 13.40 percent 1999 government stock traded on Monday at 104.35 rupees against its last traded 104.61, the 13.85 percent 2000 stock improved to 105.43 from 105.35 while the 13.85 percent 2001 was traded at 104.60 against 104.55.
Dealers said the January 1, 1998 treasury bill was traded at a yield of 9.1 percent.
